title: Java: == versus equals

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own lesson text and examples on java: == versus equals, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

outcomes: can predict the result of == and equals for strings and boxed numbers
can write equals and hashCode for a class of their own
can explain why HashSet and contains depend on equals

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: `if (status == "PAID")` is one of the most common Java bugs in student code, and it is cruel: it works in some tests and fails in others. "What is the difference between == and equals?" is asked in nearly every Java interview because the honest answer requires knowing how objects, references and the string pool work.

sections.heading: Two kinds of sameness
sections.body:
For objects, a Java variable holds a **reference**, an arrow to an object somewhere on the heap.

- **`a == b`** asks: do the two arrows point to **the same object**? It never looks inside.
- **`a.equals(b)`** asks: do the two objects **mean the same thing**? `String.equals` compares the characters. The default `equals` inherited from `Object` is just `==`, so your own classes compare by reference until you override it.

For primitives (`int`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`), `==` compares the values directly, which is what you want.

**String literals** are stored once in the **string pool**, so two identical literals share one object and `==` happens to be `true`. A string made at runtime (read from input, built with `StringBuilder`, created with `new`) is a separate object, so `==` is `false` even when the text matches. That is why `==` "sometimes works": it depends on where the string came from.

> **Note:** Compare strings with `equals`, or `equalsIgnoreCase` for case-insensitive text. To be safe when the variable may be null, put the constant first: `"PAID".equals(status)` is `false` for null instead of throwing `NullPointerException`.

sections.heading: Five comparisons
sections.body: Literals, `new String`, a string built at runtime, and boxed `Integer`s. The last two lines show a second trap: `Integer` values from -128 to 127 are cached, so `==` works for 127 and fails for 128.

code.expected_output:
a == b: true
a == c: false, a.equals(c): true
a == d: false, a.equals(d): true
127 == 127: true, 128 == 128: false
128 equals 128: true
code.caption: == compares references; equals compares contents

sections.heading: equals and hashCode for your own classes
sections.body:
When you create a class such as `Room(block, number)`, Java does not know that two rooms with the same block and number are "the same room". `list.contains(...)`, `indexOf`, `remove(Object)` and every hash-based collection use `equals`, so without an override they all compare references.

Override **both** `equals` and `hashCode`, always together. The **contract**: if `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must also be true. `HashSet` and `HashMap` first use the hash to find a bucket, then `equals` inside it. Equal objects with different hashes land in different buckets, so the set keeps both "copies" and `contains` may miss.

`Objects.hash(block, number)` builds a good hash from the same fields that `equals` compares. Use the same fields in both methods, and keep them `final` so an object's hash cannot change while it sits in a set.

sections.heading: A Room that knows its own equality
sections.body: `Room` overrides both methods; `PlainRoom` does not. The same `contains` call gives different answers, and the `HashSet` keeps only one of two equal rooms.

code.expected_output:
Room with equals, contains: true
PlainRoom, contains: false
HashSet of two equal rooms has size 1
code.caption: Overriding equals and hashCode for your own class

sections.heading: Planning the hands-on task
sections.body:
The task reads names from input and counts how many match a query, ignoring case. The starter compares with `==`. Every name read by `readLine()` is a **new String object**, so `n == query` is false for all of them and the count is always 0, even when the text matches exactly.

The fix is one method call: `n.equalsIgnoreCase(query)`. Trace the first test: names `Aditi`, `bilal`, `ADITI`, `Charu` and query `aditi`. `equalsIgnoreCase` matches the first and third, so the answer is 2. With `equals` (case-sensitive) it would be 0, because neither is spelled `aditi` in lower case. Read the task carefully: "ignoring case" decides which method you need.

One more check: the input lines may carry trailing spaces, which is why the program calls `trim()` before comparing. Two strings that differ only by a space are not equal under either method.

sections.heading: Where the string pool comes from
sections.body:
Why do two literals share an object at all? Strings in Java are **immutable**: once created, their characters never change. That makes sharing safe, so the compiler and JVM keep one copy of each literal in the **string pool** and point every use of `"Kaveri"` at it. This saves memory in programs that repeat the same words thousands of times.

Strings created while the program runs do not go into the pool automatically. `readLine()`, `substring`, `concat`, `StringBuilder.toString()` and `new String(...)` all give new objects. You *can* force a string into the pool with `s.intern()`, after which `s.intern() == "Kaveri"` is true, but do not use that as a way to compare strings: it is slower than `equals` for one-off checks and hides the intent.

The same idea explains the `Integer` cache. `Integer` objects are immutable too, and the JVM pre-creates the ones from -128 to 127 because small numbers are so common. Autoboxing (`Integer x = 127`) calls `Integer.valueOf`, which hands out the cached object; above 127 it creates a new one each time.

The lesson is the same in both cases: **sharing is an optimisation the JVM is allowed to do, not a guarantee your code can rely on.** Only `equals` tells you whether two values mean the same thing.

sections.heading: Common mix-ups
sections.body:
**Many students think `==` works for strings because it worked in their test.** It worked because both strings were literals from the pool. Strings from input, files or string building are separate objects.

**Many students think overriding `equals` alone is enough.** Without a matching `hashCode`, `HashSet` and `HashMap` break silently: duplicates appear and lookups fail.

**Many students think `Integer` behaves like `int`.** `Integer` is an object; `==` compares references and only seems to work for small cached values. Use `equals`, or unbox to `int`.

sections.heading: Interview questions
sections.body: Answers as a strong candidate would say them.

qa.q: Difference between == and equals in Java?
qa.a: == compares primitive values, or for objects whether two references point to the same object. equals compares logical equality as defined by the class; String compares characters, and the default from Object is the same as ==.

qa.q: Why must equals and hashCode be overridden together?
qa.a: Hash-based collections find a bucket by hashCode, then compare with equals. If equal objects had different hash codes they would land in different buckets, so a HashSet could hold duplicates and a HashMap lookup could miss.

qa.q: Why does `Integer a = 128, b = 128; a == b` print false but 127 prints true?
qa.a: Autoboxing uses Integer.valueOf, which caches values from -128 to 127. Two boxed 127s are the same cached object; two boxed 128s are separate objects, so the reference comparison fails. Use equals or compare ints.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- `==` on objects compares references; `equals` compares meaning.
- Literals share pooled objects; runtime strings do not.
- Compare strings with `equals` / `equalsIgnoreCase`, constant first if null is possible.
- Override `equals` and `hashCode` together, on the same final fields.
- Boxed `Integer` `==` only seems to work from -128 to 127.

quiz.explanation: new String creates a separate object; == compares references.

quiz.stem: `Integer a = 1000, b = 1000;` What is `a.equals(b)` and `a == b`?
quiz.explanation: equals compares values; 1000 is outside the cache, so the references differ.

quiz.stem: A class overrides equals but not hashCode. What can go wrong?
options: HashSet may keep two equal objects
quiz.explanation: Equal objects may hash to different buckets.

quiz.stem: Safest way to check `status` (may be null) against "PAID"?
quiz.explanation: Calling equals on the constant never throws for a null argument.

hands_on.title: Count the matching names
hands_on.task: Read `n`, then `n` names (one per line), then a query name. Print how many of the names equal the query **ignoring case**. The starter compares with `==`; fix `countMatches`.

revision_card.front: Java equality: == vs equals, the hashCode contract, and the Integer trap?
revision_card.back: == compares references (values for primitives); equals compares meaning. Override equals and hashCode together on the same fields. Boxed Integer == works only from -128 to 127 (cache).
